fields.name: Belize
fields.content: - Capital Belmopan and population of 397,000.

fields.name: Yukon River
fields.content: Northernmost river in the United States

fields.name: Nile River
fields.content: The longest river in the world, running from the Mediterranean Sea to Africa, spanning 11 countries. Divided into White Nile (originates from Lake Victoria in Uganda) and Blue Nile (originates from Lake Tana in Ethiopia).

fields.name: Charlotte Brontë
fields.content:
- Author of Jane Eyre
- Signed letters "Charles Thunder" because "bronte" is Greek for "thunder"
- Wrote the first psychological novel from a female perspective
- Her novels attacked Victorian classism

fields.name: James Joyce
fields.content:
- Famous Irish writer known for his unique books, a severe fear of thunderstorms, and an unusual friendship with Ernest Hemingway
- Helped open Ireland's first cinema in 1909
- Famous works: THE DUBLINERS (about everyday life in Dublin), ULYSSES (everyday life parallel structure to the Odyssey), FINNEGAN'S WAKE

fields.name: Thomas Jefferson
fields.content:
- Third US president and principal author of the Declaration of Independence
- Completed the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, which doubled the size of the United States
- Life at Monticello; the mountaintop plantation in Virginia, the plantation is now a national landmark and UNESCO World Heritage Site

fields.name: The Picture of Dorian Gray
fields.content: - Novel by Oscar Wilde: Dorian impulsively chooses to sell his soul and asks for the portrait, rather than himself, to age and fade

fields.name: James Madison
fields.content:
- Fourth president of the United States and "father of the constitution"  (also Secretary of State under Jefferson)
- Led the US through the War of 1812 against Britain, which  was caused by British restrictions on American trade, the forced recruitment of American sailors into the British Navy (Britain captured thousands of US soldiers and forced them to work on British warships), and British support for Native American tribes
- Was the shortest president (5'4, 100 lbs.)
- He was the sitting first president to "face enemy fire" in the War of 1812

fields.name: ER
fields.content:
- TV show from 1994-2009 that "launched George Clooney's career"
- Follows the staff of "Cook County General Hospital", a fictional hospital in Chicago

fields.name: Oscar Wilde
fields.content:
- Irish author, poet, and playwright (1854-1900), one of the most popular dramatists in the 1890s
- One of the greatest playwrights of the Victorian era

fields.name: Ethiopia
fields.content:
- Start of the Blue Nile (Nile River): The major river whose headwaters begin at Lake Tana in Ethiopia 
- Ethiopia uses a unique calendar that is roughly 7 to 8 years behind the Gregorian calendar and features 13 months (Orthodox Christian traditional calendar)
       - Calendar is based on a different calculation for Jesus' Birth
- Battle of Adwa (1896): Ethiopian forces defeated Italy, helping secure its status as one of the only African nations to avoid European colonization

fields.name: The Black Forest
fields.content:
- "Schwarzwald" in Germany is a large forested mountain range in southwest Germany
- Nearly adjacent over the border from Strasbourg in France
- Origin of "Black Forest Ham", a variety of cured smoked ham

fields.name: Germany
fields.content:
- Population of 83 million

Famous Rulers:
- Frederick Barbarossa, Frederick I: strengthened the Holy Roman Empire (ruled from 1155--1190)

fields.name: Frederick Barbarossa, Frederick I
fields.content:
- Frederick Barbarossa, Frederick I: strengthened the Holy Roman Empire (ruled from 1155--1190)
- Fought the Pope: He spent years fighting Italian city-states and the Papacy to limit church control over politics
- Reintroduced Roman Law: He reintroduced the Corpus Juris Civilis (Roman rule of law) to Central Europe

fields.name: A Moveable Feast
fields.content:
- Hemmingway's autobiography published posthumously in 1964 and edited by Hemingway's widow, Mary Hemingway.  
- Title comes from Hemingway’s own line: “Paris is a moveable feast.”  
- Chronicles Hemingway’s years in Paris from 1921 to 1926.  
- Includes vivid sketches of literary figures such as F. Scott Fitzgerald, Gertrude Stein, Ezra Pound, and James Joyce [Joyce would often start confrontations with people in Paris and hide behind Hemmingway].  
- Written in the 1950s but left unfinished; Mary Hemingway assembled the manuscript for publication.  
- The 2009 “Restored Edition” reinstated omitted chapters and corrected earlier editorial changes.

fields.name: Rhineland
fields.content:
- In 1815, at the Congress of Vienna, the diverse territories of the Rhineland were combined into an "independent" state under the reign of a Prussian king, known as Frederick William IV.  
- The Holy Roman Emperor Charles V launched a military campaign known as the Protestant Reformation in 1521 to rid the Rhineland of Protestant-affiliated principalities.   
- In WWI, the Treaty of Versailles forbade Germany from having any military presence near its frontier. Rhineland was demilitarized over the course of the Treaty's enforcement from 1919 to 1938.   
- The territorial status of the Rhineland has several times been influenced by military campaigns. Such as the Franco-Prussian War in 1870 and, most significantly, the Second World War in 1944.  
- The crucial role of the Rhine River in carrying goods and foodstuffs made it an object of rivalry for local states until it was neutralized by the League of Nations to avoid hostilities.

fields.name: Tom Sawyer
fields.content:
- Published in 1876 by Mark Twain (Samuel Clemens).  
- Set in the fictional town of St. Petersburg, Missouri, inspired by Hannibal, Missouri.  
- Tom lives with his Aunt Polly after his mother’s death and has a younger brother named Sid.  
- He famously convinces his friends to paint a fence for him by making the task seem appealing.  
- Tom and Huck witness a murder in a graveyard, setting the stage for their adventure.  
- The story concludes with Tom and Huck finding a treasure in a cave and becoming rich.

fields.name: Mark Twain
fields.content:
- Born Samuel Langhorne Clemens in 1835 in Florida, Missouri
- Adopted pen name "Mark Twain" from riverboat term meaning "two fathoms deep"
- Wrote classics like *The Adventures of Tom Sawyer* and *Adventures of Huckleberry Finn*
- Served as a riverboat pilot on the Mississippi River before the Civil War
- Known for his wit, social commentary, and advocacy for Native American rights
- Died in 1910, famously predicting his own death would coincide with Halley's Comet
- His birth and death years both fell during the appearance of Halley's Comet

fields.name: Saint Lucia
fields.content:
- Capital city is Castries
- Pop. 184,000
- It is home to the Pitons, twin volcanic peaks that inspired Caribbean freedom fighters.  
- The country is the only Commonwealth nation where French and English are official languages.  
- Saint Lucia ranks among the top tourist destinations in the Caribbean, known for its beaches and rainforests. Exports include bananas and beer.
- Its national flower is the orchid, specifically the Saint Lucia orchid.  
- The Pitons-Viviere National Park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.  
- Saint Lucia's name originates from Saint Lucy, the patron saint of the blind.

fields.name: Fiddler on the Roof
fields.content:
- Based on the 1958 novel 'Tevye the Dairyman' by Sholem Aleichem.
- Music and lyrics were composed by Jerry Herman with a book by Joseph Stein.
- The musical premiered on Broadway in 1964 and won nine Tony Awards.
- It tells the story of Tevye, a Jewish milkman in the village of Anatevka.
- The plot focuses on Tevye's attempts to uphold tradition while his daughters marry against his wishes.
- A 1971 film adaptation was directed by Jerome Robbins.
- The musical's iconic opening number is titled 'Tradition'.

fields.name: War of 1812
fields.content:
- The War of 1812 (1812–1815) was fought between the U.S. and Great Britain.  
- Primary causes included British naval impressment of American sailors and trade restrictions (Britain forced American sailors to work on British warships).  
- In 1814, British forces burned Washington, D.C., including the Capitol and White House.  
- The U.S. victory at the Battle of Lake Erie (1813) secured control of the Great Lakes.  
- Francis Scott Key wrote "The Star-Spangled Banner" during the British bombardment of Fort McHenry (1814).  
- The Treaty of Ghent (1814) ended the war, restoring pre-war territorial boundaries.  
- The Battle of New Orleans (1815) occurred after the treaty but before news of it reached combatants.

fields.name: Springfield, IL
fields.content:
- Springfield, IL was founded in 1819 and incorporated as a city in 1832, serving as the capital of Illinois since statehood in 1818.  
- It is located in Sangamon County along the Sangamon River in central Illinois, roughly 200 miles southwest of Chicago.  
- The city’s population is approximately 115,000 (2020 Census), making it the 7th‑largest municipality in the state.  
- The Illinois State Capitol building, a historic domed structure, is located downtown and is a major attraction.  
- Home of the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum, which preserves the 12‑acre site of Lincoln’s law office and the Rust Block.  
- The city hosts the annual “Lincoln Homecoming” events and the “Illinois State Fair” drawing thousands of visitors each summer.

fields.name: Snake River
fields.content: - Major river in the Pacific Northwest and largest tributary (a smaller stream or river that flows into a larger river or lake instead of directly into the ocean) of the Columbia River

fields.name: South Tyrol
fields.content:
- Northeastern-most region of Italy, bordering Austria and Switzerland
- Capital city is Bolzano
- Considerable autonomy, with the right to keep 90% of its revenue
- Italy's wealthiest province and among the wealthiest in the EU
- 57.6% use German as first language, 22.6% Italian, 3.7% Ladin
- Allies promised the region to Italy in the Treaty of London of 1915, to incentivize Italy to enter WWI

fields.name: Yellowstone River
fields.content:
- The Yellowstone River rises from Yellowstone Lake in Wyoming and flows 692 miles northward through Montana and into North Dakota before joining the Missouri River.  
- Flows through Yellowstone National Park.
- It is the longest tributary of the Missouri River, draining an approximate watershed of 25,000 square miles.  
- The river supports world‑renowned trout fishing, especially for Yellowstone cutthroat trout and brown trout.  
- The historic Yellowstone River Bridge near Bismarck, North Dakota, was completed in 1922 and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.  
- The Yellowstone River Canyon, a 40‑mile stretch in north‑central Montana, is a popular destination for white‑water rafting and scenic boating.

fields.name: Yellowstone (TV)
fields.content:
- Yellowstone is an American drama television series created by Taylor Sheridan and John Linson.
- It stars Kevin Costner as John Dutton, the patriarch of the Dutton family who owns the largest contiguous ranch in the United States. The ranch is the largest cattle ranch in Montana.
- The show premiered on the Paramount Network on June 20, 2018.
- The series centers on the Dutton family's struggles to protect their ranch from land developers, an Indian reservation, and a national park.
- The show features an ensemble cast including Luke Grimes, Kelly Reilly, Wes Bentley, and Cole Hauser.
- Yellowstone was renewed for a fifth and final season, which is being split into two parts.
- The series has spawned multiple prequel spin-offs, including 1923 and 1924.

fields.name: Francis Scott Key
fields.content:
- Francis Scott Key was an American lawyer, author, and amateur poet from Maryland.
- He played a direct role in the War of 1812 by negotiating the release of a captured American doctor, Dr. William Beanes, from British forces in 1814.
- He was detained aboard a British ship during the Battle of Baltimore because he had witnessed British military plans.
- While held on the ship, he watched the British bombardment of Fort McHenry throughout the night of September 13–14, 1814.
- The sight of the American flag still flying over Fort McHenry after the bombardment inspired him to write the poem "Defence of Fort M'Henry."
- The poem was later set to the tune of a popular British song and renamed "The Star-Spangled Banner."
- "The Star-Spangled Banner" officially became the national anthem of the United States in 1931.

fields.name: Cicero
fields.content:
- Roman statesman, lawyer, and philosopher (106 BC – 43 BC)
- Born 106 BC in Arpinum, Cicero rose to prominence as a leading orator and lawyer in the late Roman Republic.  
- He served as consul in 63 BC, famously exposing the Catiline Conspiracy and preserving the Republic’s stability.  
- Cicero’s Philippic speeches were pivotal in the political struggle against Julius Caesar and the rise of autocracy.  
- He authored the first systematic treatise on Roman rhetoric, shaping Western literary and rhetorical theory for centuries.  
- His philosophical works, such as *De Republica* and *De Legibus*, laid foundational ideas for natural law and republican governance.  
- Cicero’s polished Latin prose set the standard for classical Latin literature and was studied by scholars for generations.  
- Executed in 43 BC by the Second Triumvirate, he became a martyr for republican ideals and a symbol of resistance to tyranny.

fields.name: Siegfried Line
fields.content:
- The Siegfried Line was a extensive system of German defensive fortifications built along Germany's western border with France, constructed in the 1930s as part of Nazi rearmament.  
- It stretched approximately 650 kilometers (400 miles) from the Rhine River to the Swiss border, featuring bunkers, tank barriers, and anti-tank ditches.  
- The line was intended to protect Germany's western frontier and mirror the French Maginot Line, but it proved largely obsolete during World War II after the German invasion of France in 1940.  
- During the Battle of the Bulge in late 1944, U.S. forces encountered remnants of the fortified line, using some positions as defensive strongpoints in harsh winter conditions.  
- After the war, parts of the Siegfried Line were reused by the French as defensive positions during the Cold War, reflecting its continued strategic relevance.  
- The name "Siegfried Line" derives from the 19th-century German legend of the hero Siegfried, symbolizing national strength and defense.  
- Today, sections of the line are preserved as historical memorials and museums, offering insight into 20th-century military engineering and European history.

fields.name: Battle of the Bulge
fields.content:
- Also known as the Ardennes Offensive, this was an Axis offensive campaign on Europe's western front from Dec 1944 - Jan 1945
- Was launched in the densely forreseted region of Ardennes, Belgium and northern Luxembourg.
- Purpose was to stop Allied use of the port at Antwerp.
- During the battle, U.S. forces encountered remnants of the Siegfried Line, using some positions as defensive strongpoints in harsh winter conditions.

fields.name: Marie Curie
fields.content:
- Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, Poland, in 1867.
- First woman to win a Nobel Prize and only person to win in two scientific fields.
- Discovered the radioactive elements polonium (named after Poland) and radium.
- Co‑authored the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with her husband Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel.
- Established the first laboratory for radioactivity research in Paris, known as the Curie Institute.
- Died in 1934 from aplastic anemia caused by prolonged radiation exposure.

fields.name: Italy
fields.content:
- "The Alps" divide Switzerland and Italy, with the Matterhorn being one of the highest peaks in this range.
- The Adriatic Sea separates the Italian Peninsula from the Balkan Peninsula.
- Galileo: famous Italian astronomer, physicist, and engineer who helped start modern science. He was born in Pisa, Italy, on February 15, 1564, and died on January 8, 1642. Inventions include the telescope, discovering the four main moons of Jupiter, supported Heliocentrism (supporting Copernicus' theory).
